How to read this board

Two kinds of evidence appear here, and they are not equal.

Verified numbers come from real Pokémon Showdown battles played under the current ruleset — the engine the game is actually played on. These are the numbers that count.

Practice sim numbers come from a fast approximate simulator the lab uses to scout habits: which four get picked, who leads, what moves open the game. Good for reading tendencies, but hypotheses only — a practice-sim number is never proof and is always labelled.

Confidence chips grade the verified sample: Strong evidence means 500+ verified games against 8+ different opponents; Established 200+ against 6+; Still developing 60+ against 3+; Early anything less. “Scouting probe out of date” means the habit data was recorded before the latest rules update — the verified record itself is always current.

A “game” is counted from this team’s side of a battle. “Picked” means chosen among the four Pokémon actually brought to a battle — teams register six, only four play.

Fine print — what these numbers can and can’t say

  • 6,984 Showdown games played under older rules or an older lab setup are kept as historical context only; they do not count toward the verified record or the confidence grade.
  • Knockout shares, damage shares, opening moves, and the sim matchup hypotheses come from the fast practice simulator. The slot-weight table uses verified Showdown games when available. The two data sets are labelled with their own game counts because they measure different things — their numbers will not match.
  • Matchup playbooks describe what the team repeatedly chose against each opponent in practice-sim scouting. They do not claim the most-used bring or lead causally outperforms the alternatives.
  • Picked-versus-benched win rates are observational: a Pokémon saved for the hardest matchups can look harmful when it is actually doing the hardest work. A negative swing is a question to investigate, not a verdict.
  • Older-rules context: 6,984 earlier games at 72.0% won; excluded from the headline record and the confidence grade.

How to read this report

Two kinds of evidence appear here, and they are not equal.

Verified numbers come from real Pokémon Showdown battles played under the current ruleset — the engine the game is actually played on. These are the numbers that count.

Practice sim numbers come from a fast approximate simulator the lab uses to scout habits: which four get picked, who leads, what moves open the game. Good for reading tendencies, but hypotheses only — a practice-sim number is never proof and is always labelled.

Confidence chips grade the verified sample: Strong evidence means 500+ verified games against 8+ different opponents; Established 200+ against 6+; Still developing 60+ against 3+; Early anything less. “Scouting probe out of date” means the habit data was recorded before the latest rules update — the verified record itself is always current.

A “game” is counted from this team’s side of a battle. “Picked” means chosen among the four Pokémon actually brought to a battle — teams register six, only four play.

Fine print — what these numbers can and can’t say

  • 24,090 Showdown games played under older rules or an older lab setup are kept as historical context only; they do not count toward the verified record or the confidence grade.
  • Knockout shares, damage shares, opening moves, and the sim matchup hypotheses come from the fast practice simulator. The slot-weight table uses verified Showdown games when available. The two data sets are labelled with their own game counts because they measure different things — their numbers will not match.
  • Matchup playbooks describe what the team repeatedly chose against each opponent in practice-sim scouting. They do not claim the most-used bring or lead causally outperforms the alternatives.
  • Picked-versus-benched win rates are observational: a Pokémon saved for the hardest matchups can look harmful when it is actually doing the hardest work. A negative swing is a question to investigate, not a verdict.
  • Older-rules context: 24,090 earlier games at 65.9% won; excluded from the headline record and the confidence grade.

How to read this report

Two kinds of evidence appear here, and they are not equal.

Verified numbers come from real Pokémon Showdown battles played under the current ruleset — the engine the game is actually played on. These are the numbers that count.

Practice sim numbers come from a fast approximate simulator the lab uses to scout habits: which four get picked, who leads, what moves open the game. Good for reading tendencies, but hypotheses only — a practice-sim number is never proof and is always labelled.

Confidence chips grade the verified sample: Strong evidence means 500+ verified games against 8+ different opponents; Established 200+ against 6+; Still developing 60+ against 3+; Early anything less. “Scouting probe out of date” means the habit data was recorded before the latest rules update — the verified record itself is always current.

A “game” is counted from this team’s side of a battle. “Picked” means chosen among the four Pokémon actually brought to a battle — teams register six, only four play.

Fine print — what these numbers can and can’t say

  • 19,632 Showdown games played under older rules or an older lab setup are kept as historical context only; they do not count toward the verified record or the confidence grade.
  • Knockout shares, damage shares, opening moves, and the sim matchup hypotheses come from the fast practice simulator. The slot-weight table uses verified Showdown games when available. The two data sets are labelled with their own game counts because they measure different things — their numbers will not match.
  • Matchup playbooks describe what the team repeatedly chose against each opponent in practice-sim scouting. They do not claim the most-used bring or lead causally outperforms the alternatives.
  • Picked-versus-benched win rates are observational: a Pokémon saved for the hardest matchups can look harmful when it is actually doing the hardest work. A negative swing is a question to investigate, not a verdict.
  • Older-rules context: 19,632 earlier games at 69.1% won; excluded from the headline record and the confidence grade.

How to read this report

Two kinds of evidence appear here, and they are not equal.

Verified numbers come from real Pokémon Showdown battles played under the current ruleset — the engine the game is actually played on. These are the numbers that count.

Practice sim numbers come from a fast approximate simulator the lab uses to scout habits: which four get picked, who leads, what moves open the game. Good for reading tendencies, but hypotheses only — a practice-sim number is never proof and is always labelled.

Confidence chips grade the verified sample: Strong evidence means 500+ verified games against 8+ different opponents; Established 200+ against 6+; Still developing 60+ against 3+; Early anything less. “Scouting probe out of date” means the habit data was recorded before the latest rules update — the verified record itself is always current.

A “game” is counted from this team’s side of a battle. “Picked” means chosen among the four Pokémon actually brought to a battle — teams register six, only four play.

Fine print — what these numbers can and can’t say

  • 6,276 Showdown games played under older rules or an older lab setup are kept as historical context only; they do not count toward the verified record or the confidence grade.
  • Knockout shares, damage shares, opening moves, and the sim matchup hypotheses come from the fast practice simulator. The slot-weight table uses verified Showdown games when available. The two data sets are labelled with their own game counts because they measure different things — their numbers will not match.
  • Matchup playbooks describe what the team repeatedly chose against each opponent in practice-sim scouting. They do not claim the most-used bring or lead causally outperforms the alternatives.
  • Picked-versus-benched win rates are observational: a Pokémon saved for the hardest matchups can look harmful when it is actually doing the hardest work. A negative swing is a question to investigate, not a verdict.
  • Older-rules context: 6,276 earlier games at 68.9% won; excluded from the headline record and the confidence grade.

How to read this report

Two kinds of evidence appear here, and they are not equal.

Verified numbers come from real Pokémon Showdown battles played under the current ruleset — the engine the game is actually played on. These are the numbers that count.

Practice sim numbers come from a fast approximate simulator the lab uses to scout habits: which four get picked, who leads, what moves open the game. Good for reading tendencies, but hypotheses only — a practice-sim number is never proof and is always labelled.

Confidence chips grade the verified sample: Strong evidence means 500+ verified games against 8+ different opponents; Established 200+ against 6+; Still developing 60+ against 3+; Early anything less. “Scouting probe out of date” means the habit data was recorded before the latest rules update — the verified record itself is always current.

A “game” is counted from this team’s side of a battle. “Picked” means chosen among the four Pokémon actually brought to a battle — teams register six, only four play.

Fine print — what these numbers can and can’t say

  • 51,606 Showdown games played under older rules or an older lab setup are kept as historical context only; they do not count toward the verified record or the confidence grade.
  • Knockout shares, damage shares, opening moves, and the sim matchup hypotheses come from the fast practice simulator. The slot-weight table uses verified Showdown games when available. The two data sets are labelled with their own game counts because they measure different things — their numbers will not match.
  • Matchup playbooks describe what the team repeatedly chose against each opponent in practice-sim scouting. They do not claim the most-used bring or lead causally outperforms the alternatives.
  • Picked-versus-benched win rates are observational: a Pokémon saved for the hardest matchups can look harmful when it is actually doing the hardest work. A negative swing is a question to investigate, not a verdict.
  • Older-rules context: 51,606 earlier games at 69.6% won; excluded from the headline record and the confidence grade.

How to read this report

Two kinds of evidence appear here, and they are not equal.

Verified numbers come from real Pokémon Showdown battles played under the current ruleset — the engine the game is actually played on. These are the numbers that count.

Practice sim numbers come from a fast approximate simulator the lab uses to scout habits: which four get picked, who leads, what moves open the game. Good for reading tendencies, but hypotheses only — a practice-sim number is never proof and is always labelled.

Confidence chips grade the verified sample: Strong evidence means 500+ verified games against 8+ different opponents; Established 200+ against 6+; Still developing 60+ against 3+; Early anything less. “Scouting probe out of date” means the habit data was recorded before the latest rules update — the verified record itself is always current.

A “game” is counted from this team’s side of a battle. “Picked” means chosen among the four Pokémon actually brought to a battle — teams register six, only four play.

Fine print — what these numbers can and can’t say

  • 2,394 Showdown games played under older rules or an older lab setup are kept as historical context only; they do not count toward the verified record or the confidence grade.
  • Knockout shares, damage shares, opening moves, and the sim matchup hypotheses come from the fast practice simulator. The slot-weight table uses verified Showdown games when available. The two data sets are labelled with their own game counts because they measure different things — their numbers will not match.
  • Matchup playbooks describe what the team repeatedly chose against each opponent in practice-sim scouting. They do not claim the most-used bring or lead causally outperforms the alternatives.
  • Picked-versus-benched win rates are observational: a Pokémon saved for the hardest matchups can look harmful when it is actually doing the hardest work. A negative swing is a question to investigate, not a verdict.
  • Older-rules context: 2,394 earlier games at 61.5% won; excluded from the headline record and the confidence grade.

How to read this report

Two kinds of evidence appear here, and they are not equal.

Verified numbers come from real Pokémon Showdown battles played under the current ruleset — the engine the game is actually played on. These are the numbers that count.

Practice sim numbers come from a fast approximate simulator the lab uses to scout habits: which four get picked, who leads, what moves open the game. Good for reading tendencies, but hypotheses only — a practice-sim number is never proof and is always labelled.

Confidence chips grade the verified sample: Strong evidence means 500+ verified games against 8+ different opponents; Established 200+ against 6+; Still developing 60+ against 3+; Early anything less. “Scouting probe out of date” means the habit data was recorded before the latest rules update — the verified record itself is always current.

A “game” is counted from this team’s side of a battle. “Picked” means chosen among the four Pokémon actually brought to a battle — teams register six, only four play.

Fine print — what these numbers can and can’t say

  • 174 Showdown games played under older rules or an older lab setup are kept as historical context only; they do not count toward the verified record or the confidence grade.
  • Knockout shares, damage shares, opening moves, and the sim matchup hypotheses come from the fast practice simulator. The slot-weight table uses verified Showdown games when available. The two data sets are labelled with their own game counts because they measure different things — their numbers will not match.
  • Matchup playbooks describe what the team repeatedly chose against each opponent in practice-sim scouting. They do not claim the most-used bring or lead causally outperforms the alternatives.
  • Picked-versus-benched win rates are observational: a Pokémon saved for the hardest matchups can look harmful when it is actually doing the hardest work. A negative swing is a question to investigate, not a verdict.
  • Older-rules context: 174 earlier games at 82.8% won; excluded from the headline record and the confidence grade.

How to read this report

Two kinds of evidence appear here, and they are not equal.

Verified numbers come from real Pokémon Showdown battles played under the current ruleset — the engine the game is actually played on. These are the numbers that count.

Practice sim numbers come from a fast approximate simulator the lab uses to scout habits: which four get picked, who leads, what moves open the game. Good for reading tendencies, but hypotheses only — a practice-sim number is never proof and is always labelled.

Confidence chips grade the verified sample: Strong evidence means 500+ verified games against 8+ different opponents; Established 200+ against 6+; Still developing 60+ against 3+; Early anything less. “Scouting probe out of date” means the habit data was recorded before the latest rules update — the verified record itself is always current.

A “game” is counted from this team’s side of a battle. “Picked” means chosen among the four Pokémon actually brought to a battle — teams register six, only four play.

Read with care: a Pokémon is benched only in the matchups where benching looks right, so these comparisons show correlation, not cause. “Wins more when benched” is flagged only on a solid benched sample (at least 200 benched games, or 2% of games with a minimum of 50); below that the swing is shown but not flagged. “Rarely picked” marks slots that almost never make the four brought to battle. The definitive per-slot test is node cli.js roster-ablate <team> <slot>.

Fine print — what these numbers can and can’t say

  • Knockout shares, damage shares, opening moves, and the sim matchup hypotheses come from the fast practice simulator. The slot-weight table uses verified Showdown games when available. The two data sets are labelled with their own game counts because they measure different things — their numbers will not match.
  • Matchup playbooks describe what the team repeatedly chose against each opponent in practice-sim scouting. They do not claim the most-used bring or lead causally outperforms the alternatives.
  • Picked-versus-benched win rates are observational: a Pokémon saved for the hardest matchups can look harmful when it is actually doing the hardest work. A negative swing is a question to investigate, not a verdict.

How to read this report

Two kinds of evidence appear here, and they are not equal.

Verified numbers come from real Pokémon Showdown battles played under the current ruleset — the engine the game is actually played on. These are the numbers that count.

Practice sim numbers come from a fast approximate simulator the lab uses to scout habits: which four get picked, who leads, what moves open the game. Good for reading tendencies, but hypotheses only — a practice-sim number is never proof and is always labelled.

Confidence chips grade the verified sample: Strong evidence means 500+ verified games against 8+ different opponents; Established 200+ against 6+; Still developing 60+ against 3+; Early anything less. “Scouting probe out of date” means the habit data was recorded before the latest rules update — the verified record itself is always current.

A “game” is counted from this team’s side of a battle. “Picked” means chosen among the four Pokémon actually brought to a battle — teams register six, only four play.

Fine print — what these numbers can and can’t say

  • 216 Showdown games played under older rules or an older lab setup are kept as historical context only; they do not count toward the verified record or the confidence grade.
  • Knockout shares, damage shares, opening moves, and the sim matchup hypotheses come from the fast practice simulator. The slot-weight table uses verified Showdown games when available. The two data sets are labelled with their own game counts because they measure different things — their numbers will not match.
  • Matchup playbooks describe what the team repeatedly chose against each opponent in practice-sim scouting. They do not claim the most-used bring or lead causally outperforms the alternatives.
  • Picked-versus-benched win rates are observational: a Pokémon saved for the hardest matchups can look harmful when it is actually doing the hardest work. A negative swing is a question to investigate, not a verdict.
  • Older-rules context: 216 earlier games at 68.5% won; excluded from the headline record and the confidence grade.

How to read this report

Two kinds of evidence appear here, and they are not equal.

Verified numbers come from real Pokémon Showdown battles played under the current ruleset — the engine the game is actually played on. These are the numbers that count.

Practice sim numbers come from a fast approximate simulator the lab uses to scout habits: which four get picked, who leads, what moves open the game. Good for reading tendencies, but hypotheses only — a practice-sim number is never proof and is always labelled.

Confidence chips grade the verified sample: Strong evidence means 500+ verified games against 8+ different opponents; Established 200+ against 6+; Still developing 60+ against 3+; Early anything less. “Scouting probe out of date” means the habit data was recorded before the latest rules update — the verified record itself is always current.

A “game” is counted from this team’s side of a battle. “Picked” means chosen among the four Pokémon actually brought to a battle — teams register six, only four play.

Fine print — what these numbers can and can’t say

  • 24,906 Showdown games played under older rules or an older lab setup are kept as historical context only; they do not count toward the verified record or the confidence grade.
  • Knockout shares, damage shares, opening moves, and the sim matchup hypotheses come from the fast practice simulator. The slot-weight table uses verified Showdown games when available. The two data sets are labelled with their own game counts because they measure different things — their numbers will not match.
  • Matchup playbooks describe what the team repeatedly chose against each opponent in practice-sim scouting. They do not claim the most-used bring or lead causally outperforms the alternatives.
  • Picked-versus-benched win rates are observational: a Pokémon saved for the hardest matchups can look harmful when it is actually doing the hardest work. A negative swing is a question to investigate, not a verdict.
  • Older-rules context: 24,906 earlier games at 68.1% won; excluded from the headline record and the confidence grade.

How to read this report

Two kinds of evidence appear here, and they are not equal.

Verified numbers come from real Pokémon Showdown battles played under the current ruleset — the engine the game is actually played on. These are the numbers that count.

Practice sim numbers come from a fast approximate simulator the lab uses to scout habits: which four get picked, who leads, what moves open the game. Good for reading tendencies, but hypotheses only — a practice-sim number is never proof and is always labelled.

Confidence chips grade the verified sample: Strong evidence means 500+ verified games against 8+ different opponents; Established 200+ against 6+; Still developing 60+ against 3+; Early anything less. “Scouting probe out of date” means the habit data was recorded before the latest rules update — the verified record itself is always current.

A “game” is counted from this team’s side of a battle. “Picked” means chosen among the four Pokémon actually brought to a battle — teams register six, only four play.

Fine print — what these numbers can and can’t say

  • 26,958 Showdown games played under older rules or an older lab setup are kept as historical context only; they do not count toward the verified record or the confidence grade.
  • Knockout shares, damage shares, opening moves, and the sim matchup hypotheses come from the fast practice simulator. The slot-weight table uses verified Showdown games when available. The two data sets are labelled with their own game counts because they measure different things — their numbers will not match.
  • Matchup playbooks describe what the team repeatedly chose against each opponent in practice-sim scouting. They do not claim the most-used bring or lead causally outperforms the alternatives.
  • Picked-versus-benched win rates are observational: a Pokémon saved for the hardest matchups can look harmful when it is actually doing the hardest work. A negative swing is a question to investigate, not a verdict.
  • Older-rules context: 26,958 earlier games at 65.9% won; excluded from the headline record and the confidence grade.

How to read this report

Two kinds of evidence appear here, and they are not equal.

Verified numbers come from real Pokémon Showdown battles played under the current ruleset — the engine the game is actually played on. These are the numbers that count.

Practice sim numbers come from a fast approximate simulator the lab uses to scout habits: which four get picked, who leads, what moves open the game. Good for reading tendencies, but hypotheses only — a practice-sim number is never proof and is always labelled.

Confidence chips grade the verified sample: Strong evidence means 500+ verified games against 8+ different opponents; Established 200+ against 6+; Still developing 60+ against 3+; Early anything less. “Scouting probe out of date” means the habit data was recorded before the latest rules update — the verified record itself is always current.

A “game” is counted from this team’s side of a battle. “Picked” means chosen among the four Pokémon actually brought to a battle — teams register six, only four play.

Fine print — what these numbers can and can’t say

  • 30 Showdown games played under older rules or an older lab setup are kept as historical context only; they do not count toward the verified record or the confidence grade.
  • Knockout shares, damage shares, opening moves, and the sim matchup hypotheses come from the fast practice simulator. The slot-weight table uses verified Showdown games when available. The two data sets are labelled with their own game counts because they measure different things — their numbers will not match.
  • Matchup playbooks describe what the team repeatedly chose against each opponent in practice-sim scouting. They do not claim the most-used bring or lead causally outperforms the alternatives.
  • Picked-versus-benched win rates are observational: a Pokémon saved for the hardest matchups can look harmful when it is actually doing the hardest work. A negative swing is a question to investigate, not a verdict.
  • Older-rules context: 30 earlier games at 26.7% won; excluded from the headline record and the confidence grade.

How to read this report

Two kinds of evidence appear here, and they are not equal.

Verified numbers come from real Pokémon Showdown battles played under the current ruleset — the engine the game is actually played on. These are the numbers that count.

Practice sim numbers come from a fast approximate simulator the lab uses to scout habits: which four get picked, who leads, what moves open the game. Good for reading tendencies, but hypotheses only — a practice-sim number is never proof and is always labelled.

Confidence chips grade the verified sample: Strong evidence means 500+ verified games against 8+ different opponents; Established 200+ against 6+; Still developing 60+ against 3+; Early anything less. “Scouting probe out of date” means the habit data was recorded before the latest rules update — the verified record itself is always current.

A “game” is counted from this team’s side of a battle. “Picked” means chosen among the four Pokémon actually brought to a battle — teams register six, only four play.

Fine print — what these numbers can and can’t say

  • 21,666 Showdown games played under older rules or an older lab setup are kept as historical context only; they do not count toward the verified record or the confidence grade.
  • Knockout shares, damage shares, opening moves, and the sim matchup hypotheses come from the fast practice simulator. The slot-weight table uses verified Showdown games when available. The two data sets are labelled with their own game counts because they measure different things — their numbers will not match.
  • Matchup playbooks describe what the team repeatedly chose against each opponent in practice-sim scouting. They do not claim the most-used bring or lead causally outperforms the alternatives.
  • Picked-versus-benched win rates are observational: a Pokémon saved for the hardest matchups can look harmful when it is actually doing the hardest work. A negative swing is a question to investigate, not a verdict.
  • Older-rules context: 21,666 earlier games at 63.6% won; excluded from the headline record and the confidence grade.

How to read this report

Two kinds of evidence appear here, and they are not equal.

Verified numbers come from real Pokémon Showdown battles played under the current ruleset — the engine the game is actually played on. These are the numbers that count.

Practice sim numbers come from a fast approximate simulator the lab uses to scout habits: which four get picked, who leads, what moves open the game. Good for reading tendencies, but hypotheses only — a practice-sim number is never proof and is always labelled.

Confidence chips grade the verified sample: Strong evidence means 500+ verified games against 8+ different opponents; Established 200+ against 6+; Still developing 60+ against 3+; Early anything less. “Scouting probe out of date” means the habit data was recorded before the latest rules update — the verified record itself is always current.

A “game” is counted from this team’s side of a battle. “Picked” means chosen among the four Pokémon actually brought to a battle — teams register six, only four play.

Fine print — what these numbers can and can’t say

  • 1,050 Showdown games played under older rules or an older lab setup are kept as historical context only; they do not count toward the verified record or the confidence grade.
  • Knockout shares, damage shares, opening moves, and the sim matchup hypotheses come from the fast practice simulator. The slot-weight table uses verified Showdown games when available. The two data sets are labelled with their own game counts because they measure different things — their numbers will not match.
  • Matchup playbooks describe what the team repeatedly chose against each opponent in practice-sim scouting. They do not claim the most-used bring or lead causally outperforms the alternatives.
  • Picked-versus-benched win rates are observational: a Pokémon saved for the hardest matchups can look harmful when it is actually doing the hardest work. A negative swing is a question to investigate, not a verdict.
  • Older-rules context: 1,050 earlier games at 63.4% won; excluded from the headline record and the confidence grade.

How to read this report

Two kinds of evidence appear here, and they are not equal.

Verified numbers come from real Pokémon Showdown battles played under the current ruleset — the engine the game is actually played on. These are the numbers that count.

Practice sim numbers come from a fast approximate simulator the lab uses to scout habits: which four get picked, who leads, what moves open the game. Good for reading tendencies, but hypotheses only — a practice-sim number is never proof and is always labelled.

Confidence chips grade the verified sample: Strong evidence means 500+ verified games against 8+ different opponents; Established 200+ against 6+; Still developing 60+ against 3+; Early anything less. “Scouting probe out of date” means the habit data was recorded before the latest rules update — the verified record itself is always current.

A “game” is counted from this team’s side of a battle. “Picked” means chosen among the four Pokémon actually brought to a battle — teams register six, only four play.

Fine print — what these numbers can and can’t say

  • Knockout shares, damage shares, opening moves, and the sim matchup hypotheses come from the fast practice simulator. The slot-weight table uses verified Showdown games when available. The two data sets are labelled with their own game counts because they measure different things — their numbers will not match.
  • Matchup playbooks describe what the team repeatedly chose against each opponent in practice-sim scouting. They do not claim the most-used bring or lead causally outperforms the alternatives.
  • Picked-versus-benched win rates are observational: a Pokémon saved for the hardest matchups can look harmful when it is actually doing the hardest work. A negative swing is a question to investigate, not a verdict.

How to read this report

Two kinds of evidence appear here, and they are not equal.

Verified numbers come from real Pokémon Showdown battles played under the current ruleset — the engine the game is actually played on. These are the numbers that count.

Practice sim numbers come from a fast approximate simulator the lab uses to scout habits: which four get picked, who leads, what moves open the game. Good for reading tendencies, but hypotheses only — a practice-sim number is never proof and is always labelled.

Confidence chips grade the verified sample: Strong evidence means 500+ verified games against 8+ different opponents; Established 200+ against 6+; Still developing 60+ against 3+; Early anything less. “Scouting probe out of date” means the habit data was recorded before the latest rules update — the verified record itself is always current.

A “game” is counted from this team’s side of a battle. “Picked” means chosen among the four Pokémon actually brought to a battle — teams register six, only four play.

Fine print — what these numbers can and can’t say

  • 882 Showdown games played under older rules or an older lab setup are kept as historical context only; they do not count toward the verified record or the confidence grade.
  • Knockout shares, damage shares, opening moves, and the sim matchup hypotheses come from the fast practice simulator. The slot-weight table uses verified Showdown games when available. The two data sets are labelled with their own game counts because they measure different things — their numbers will not match.
  • Matchup playbooks describe what the team repeatedly chose against each opponent in practice-sim scouting. They do not claim the most-used bring or lead causally outperforms the alternatives.
  • Picked-versus-benched win rates are observational: a Pokémon saved for the hardest matchups can look harmful when it is actually doing the hardest work. A negative swing is a question to investigate, not a verdict.
  • Older-rules context: 882 earlier games at 74.1% won; excluded from the headline record and the confidence grade.

How to read this report

Two kinds of evidence appear here, and they are not equal.

Verified numbers come from real Pokémon Showdown battles played under the current ruleset — the engine the game is actually played on. These are the numbers that count.

Practice sim numbers come from a fast approximate simulator the lab uses to scout habits: which four get picked, who leads, what moves open the game. Good for reading tendencies, but hypotheses only — a practice-sim number is never proof and is always labelled.

Confidence chips grade the verified sample: Strong evidence means 500+ verified games against 8+ different opponents; Established 200+ against 6+; Still developing 60+ against 3+; Early anything less. “Scouting probe out of date” means the habit data was recorded before the latest rules update — the verified record itself is always current.

A “game” is counted from this team’s side of a battle. “Picked” means chosen among the four Pokémon actually brought to a battle — teams register six, only four play.

Fine print — what these numbers can and can’t say

  • Knockout shares, damage shares, opening moves, and the sim matchup hypotheses come from the fast practice simulator. The slot-weight table uses verified Showdown games when available. The two data sets are labelled with their own game counts because they measure different things — their numbers will not match.
  • Matchup playbooks describe what the team repeatedly chose against each opponent in practice-sim scouting. They do not claim the most-used bring or lead causally outperforms the alternatives.
  • Picked-versus-benched win rates are observational: a Pokémon saved for the hardest matchups can look harmful when it is actually doing the hardest work. A negative swing is a question to investigate, not a verdict.

How to read this report

Two kinds of evidence appear here, and they are not equal.

Verified numbers come from real Pokémon Showdown battles played under the current ruleset — the engine the game is actually played on. These are the numbers that count.

Practice sim numbers come from a fast approximate simulator the lab uses to scout habits: which four get picked, who leads, what moves open the game. Good for reading tendencies, but hypotheses only — a practice-sim number is never proof and is always labelled.

Confidence chips grade the verified sample: Strong evidence means 500+ verified games against 8+ different opponents; Established 200+ against 6+; Still developing 60+ against 3+; Early anything less. “Scouting probe out of date” means the habit data was recorded before the latest rules update — the verified record itself is always current.

A “game” is counted from this team’s side of a battle. “Picked” means chosen among the four Pokémon actually brought to a battle — teams register six, only four play.

Fine print — what these numbers can and can’t say

  • 102 Showdown games played under older rules or an older lab setup are kept as historical context only; they do not count toward the verified record or the confidence grade.
  • Knockout shares, damage shares, opening moves, and the sim matchup hypotheses come from the fast practice simulator. The slot-weight table uses verified Showdown games when available. The two data sets are labelled with their own game counts because they measure different things — their numbers will not match.
  • Matchup playbooks describe what the team repeatedly chose against each opponent in practice-sim scouting. They do not claim the most-used bring or lead causally outperforms the alternatives.
  • Picked-versus-benched win rates are observational: a Pokémon saved for the hardest matchups can look harmful when it is actually doing the hardest work. A negative swing is a question to investigate, not a verdict.
  • Older-rules context: 102 earlier games at 83.3% won; excluded from the headline record and the confidence grade.

How to read this report

Two kinds of evidence appear here, and they are not equal.

Verified numbers come from real Pokémon Showdown battles played under the current ruleset — the engine the game is actually played on. These are the numbers that count.

Practice sim numbers come from a fast approximate simulator the lab uses to scout habits: which four get picked, who leads, what moves open the game. Good for reading tendencies, but hypotheses only — a practice-sim number is never proof and is always labelled.

Confidence chips grade the verified sample: Strong evidence means 500+ verified games against 8+ different opponents; Established 200+ against 6+; Still developing 60+ against 3+; Early anything less. “Scouting probe out of date” means the habit data was recorded before the latest rules update — the verified record itself is always current.

A “game” is counted from this team’s side of a battle. “Picked” means chosen among the four Pokémon actually brought to a battle — teams register six, only four play.

Fine print — what these numbers can and can’t say

  • Knockout shares, damage shares, opening moves, and the sim matchup hypotheses come from the fast practice simulator. The slot-weight table uses verified Showdown games when available. The two data sets are labelled with their own game counts because they measure different things — their numbers will not match.
  • Matchup playbooks describe what the team repeatedly chose against each opponent in practice-sim scouting. They do not claim the most-used bring or lead causally outperforms the alternatives.
  • Picked-versus-benched win rates are observational: a Pokémon saved for the hardest matchups can look harmful when it is actually doing the hardest work. A negative swing is a question to investigate, not a verdict.

How to read this report

Two kinds of evidence appear here, and they are not equal.

Verified numbers come from real Pokémon Showdown battles played under the current ruleset — the engine the game is actually played on. These are the numbers that count.

Practice sim numbers come from a fast approximate simulator the lab uses to scout habits: which four get picked, who leads, what moves open the game. Good for reading tendencies, but hypotheses only — a practice-sim number is never proof and is always labelled.

Confidence chips grade the verified sample: Strong evidence means 500+ verified games against 8+ different opponents; Established 200+ against 6+; Still developing 60+ against 3+; Early anything less. “Scouting probe out of date” means the habit data was recorded before the latest rules update — the verified record itself is always current.

A “game” is counted from this team’s side of a battle. “Picked” means chosen among the four Pokémon actually brought to a battle — teams register six, only four play.

Fine print — what these numbers can and can’t say

  • Knockout shares, damage shares, opening moves, and the sim matchup hypotheses come from the fast practice simulator. The slot-weight table uses verified Showdown games when available. The two data sets are labelled with their own game counts because they measure different things — their numbers will not match.
  • Matchup playbooks describe what the team repeatedly chose against each opponent in practice-sim scouting. They do not claim the most-used bring or lead causally outperforms the alternatives.
  • Picked-versus-benched win rates are observational: a Pokémon saved for the hardest matchups can look harmful when it is actually doing the hardest work. A negative swing is a question to investigate, not a verdict.

How to read this report

Two kinds of evidence appear here, and they are not equal.

Verified numbers come from real Pokémon Showdown battles played under the current ruleset — the engine the game is actually played on. These are the numbers that count.

Practice sim numbers come from a fast approximate simulator the lab uses to scout habits: which four get picked, who leads, what moves open the game. Good for reading tendencies, but hypotheses only — a practice-sim number is never proof and is always labelled.

Confidence chips grade the verified sample: Strong evidence means 500+ verified games against 8+ different opponents; Established 200+ against 6+; Still developing 60+ against 3+; Early anything less. “Scouting probe out of date” means the habit data was recorded before the latest rules update — the verified record itself is always current.

A “game” is counted from this team’s side of a battle. “Picked” means chosen among the four Pokémon actually brought to a battle — teams register six, only four play.

Fine print — what these numbers can and can’t say

  • 26,472 Showdown games played under older rules or an older lab setup are kept as historical context only; they do not count toward the verified record or the confidence grade.
  • Knockout shares, damage shares, opening moves, and the sim matchup hypotheses come from the fast practice simulator. The slot-weight table uses verified Showdown games when available. The two data sets are labelled with their own game counts because they measure different things — their numbers will not match.
  • Matchup playbooks describe what the team repeatedly chose against each opponent in practice-sim scouting. They do not claim the most-used bring or lead causally outperforms the alternatives.
  • Picked-versus-benched win rates are observational: a Pokémon saved for the hardest matchups can look harmful when it is actually doing the hardest work. A negative swing is a question to investigate, not a verdict.
  • Older-rules context: 26,472 earlier games at 64.7% won; excluded from the headline record and the confidence grade.

How to read this report

Two kinds of evidence appear here, and they are not equal.

Verified numbers come from real Pokémon Showdown battles played under the current ruleset — the engine the game is actually played on. These are the numbers that count.

Practice sim numbers come from a fast approximate simulator the lab uses to scout habits: which four get picked, who leads, what moves open the game. Good for reading tendencies, but hypotheses only — a practice-sim number is never proof and is always labelled.

Confidence chips grade the verified sample: Strong evidence means 500+ verified games against 8+ different opponents; Established 200+ against 6+; Still developing 60+ against 3+; Early anything less. “Scouting probe out of date” means the habit data was recorded before the latest rules update — the verified record itself is always current.

A “game” is counted from this team’s side of a battle. “Picked” means chosen among the four Pokémon actually brought to a battle — teams register six, only four play.

Fine print — what these numbers can and can’t say

  • 20,682 Showdown games played under older rules or an older lab setup are kept as historical context only; they do not count toward the verified record or the confidence grade.
  • Knockout shares, damage shares, opening moves, and the sim matchup hypotheses come from the fast practice simulator. The slot-weight table uses verified Showdown games when available. The two data sets are labelled with their own game counts because they measure different things — their numbers will not match.
  • Matchup playbooks describe what the team repeatedly chose against each opponent in practice-sim scouting. They do not claim the most-used bring or lead causally outperforms the alternatives.
  • Picked-versus-benched win rates are observational: a Pokémon saved for the hardest matchups can look harmful when it is actually doing the hardest work. A negative swing is a question to investigate, not a verdict.
  • Older-rules context: 20,682 earlier games at 61.7% won; excluded from the headline record and the confidence grade.

How to read this report

Two kinds of evidence appear here, and they are not equal.

Verified numbers come from real Pokémon Showdown battles played under the current ruleset — the engine the game is actually played on. These are the numbers that count.

Practice sim numbers come from a fast approximate simulator the lab uses to scout habits: which four get picked, who leads, what moves open the game. Good for reading tendencies, but hypotheses only — a practice-sim number is never proof and is always labelled.

Confidence chips grade the verified sample: Strong evidence means 500+ verified games against 8+ different opponents; Established 200+ against 6+; Still developing 60+ against 3+; Early anything less. “Scouting probe out of date” means the habit data was recorded before the latest rules update — the verified record itself is always current.

A “game” is counted from this team’s side of a battle. “Picked” means chosen among the four Pokémon actually brought to a battle — teams register six, only four play.

Fine print — what these numbers can and can’t say

  • 72 Showdown games played under older rules or an older lab setup are kept as historical context only; they do not count toward the verified record or the confidence grade.
  • Knockout shares, damage shares, opening moves, and the sim matchup hypotheses come from the fast practice simulator. The slot-weight table uses verified Showdown games when available. The two data sets are labelled with their own game counts because they measure different things — their numbers will not match.
  • Matchup playbooks describe what the team repeatedly chose against each opponent in practice-sim scouting. They do not claim the most-used bring or lead causally outperforms the alternatives.
  • Picked-versus-benched win rates are observational: a Pokémon saved for the hardest matchups can look harmful when it is actually doing the hardest work. A negative swing is a question to investigate, not a verdict.
  • Older-rules context: 72 earlier games at 52.8% won; excluded from the headline record and the confidence grade.

How to read this report

Two kinds of evidence appear here, and they are not equal.

Verified numbers come from real Pokémon Showdown battles played under the current ruleset — the engine the game is actually played on. These are the numbers that count.

Practice sim numbers come from a fast approximate simulator the lab uses to scout habits: which four get picked, who leads, what moves open the game. Good for reading tendencies, but hypotheses only — a practice-sim number is never proof and is always labelled.

Confidence chips grade the verified sample: Strong evidence means 500+ verified games against 8+ different opponents; Established 200+ against 6+; Still developing 60+ against 3+; Early anything less. “Scouting probe out of date” means the habit data was recorded before the latest rules update — the verified record itself is always current.

A “game” is counted from this team’s side of a battle. “Picked” means chosen among the four Pokémon actually brought to a battle — teams register six, only four play.

Fine print — what these numbers can and can’t say

  • 24,390 Showdown games played under older rules or an older lab setup are kept as historical context only; they do not count toward the verified record or the confidence grade.
  • Knockout shares, damage shares, opening moves, and the sim matchup hypotheses come from the fast practice simulator. The slot-weight table uses verified Showdown games when available. The two data sets are labelled with their own game counts because they measure different things — their numbers will not match.
  • Matchup playbooks describe what the team repeatedly chose against each opponent in practice-sim scouting. They do not claim the most-used bring or lead causally outperforms the alternatives.
  • Picked-versus-benched win rates are observational: a Pokémon saved for the hardest matchups can look harmful when it is actually doing the hardest work. A negative swing is a question to investigate, not a verdict.
  • Older-rules context: 24,390 earlier games at 66.2% won; excluded from the headline record and the confidence grade.

How to read this report

Two kinds of evidence appear here, and they are not equal.

Verified numbers come from real Pokémon Showdown battles played under the current ruleset — the engine the game is actually played on. These are the numbers that count.

Practice sim numbers come from a fast approximate simulator the lab uses to scout habits: which four get picked, who leads, what moves open the game. Good for reading tendencies, but hypotheses only — a practice-sim number is never proof and is always labelled.

Confidence chips grade the verified sample: Strong evidence means 500+ verified games against 8+ different opponents; Established 200+ against 6+; Still developing 60+ against 3+; Early anything less. “Scouting probe out of date” means the habit data was recorded before the latest rules update — the verified record itself is always current.

A “game” is counted from this team’s side of a battle. “Picked” means chosen among the four Pokémon actually brought to a battle — teams register six, only four play.

Aggron: the team wins 58.9% of verified games when it sits out (953 games) versus 43.9% when it plays. That pattern can come from which matchups it gets picked for. Definitive test: node cli.js roster-ablate 85714 5.

The definitive per-slot test is node cli.js roster-ablate <team> <slot>.

Fine print — what these numbers can and can’t say

  • 25,038 Showdown games played under older rules or an older lab setup are kept as historical context only; they do not count toward the verified record or the confidence grade.
  • Knockout shares, damage shares, opening moves, and the sim matchup hypotheses come from the fast practice simulator. The slot-weight table uses verified Showdown games when available. The two data sets are labelled with their own game counts because they measure different things — their numbers will not match.
  • Matchup playbooks describe what the team repeatedly chose against each opponent in practice-sim scouting. They do not claim the most-used bring or lead causally outperforms the alternatives.
  • Picked-versus-benched win rates are observational: a Pokémon saved for the hardest matchups can look harmful when it is actually doing the hardest work. A negative swing is a question to investigate, not a verdict.
  • Older-rules context: 25,038 earlier games at 62.5% won; excluded from the headline record and the confidence grade.

How to read this report

Two kinds of evidence appear here, and they are not equal.

Verified numbers come from real Pokémon Showdown battles played under the current ruleset — the engine the game is actually played on. These are the numbers that count.

Practice sim numbers come from a fast approximate simulator the lab uses to scout habits: which four get picked, who leads, what moves open the game. Good for reading tendencies, but hypotheses only — a practice-sim number is never proof and is always labelled.

Confidence chips grade the verified sample: Strong evidence means 500+ verified games against 8+ different opponents; Established 200+ against 6+; Still developing 60+ against 3+; Early anything less. “Scouting probe out of date” means the habit data was recorded before the latest rules update — the verified record itself is always current.

A “game” is counted from this team’s side of a battle. “Picked” means chosen among the four Pokémon actually brought to a battle — teams register six, only four play.

Fine print — what these numbers can and can’t say

  • 25,938 Showdown games played under older rules or an older lab setup are kept as historical context only; they do not count toward the verified record or the confidence grade.
  • Knockout shares, damage shares, opening moves, and the sim matchup hypotheses come from the fast practice simulator. The slot-weight table uses verified Showdown games when available. The two data sets are labelled with their own game counts because they measure different things — their numbers will not match.
  • Matchup playbooks describe what the team repeatedly chose against each opponent in practice-sim scouting. They do not claim the most-used bring or lead causally outperforms the alternatives.
  • Picked-versus-benched win rates are observational: a Pokémon saved for the hardest matchups can look harmful when it is actually doing the hardest work. A negative swing is a question to investigate, not a verdict.
  • Older-rules context: 25,938 earlier games at 64.2% won; excluded from the headline record and the confidence grade.

How to read this report

Two kinds of evidence appear here, and they are not equal.

Verified numbers come from real Pokémon Showdown battles played under the current ruleset — the engine the game is actually played on. These are the numbers that count.

Practice sim numbers come from a fast approximate simulator the lab uses to scout habits: which four get picked, who leads, what moves open the game. Good for reading tendencies, but hypotheses only — a practice-sim number is never proof and is always labelled.

Confidence chips grade the verified sample: Strong evidence means 500+ verified games against 8+ different opponents; Established 200+ against 6+; Still developing 60+ against 3+; Early anything less. “Scouting probe out of date” means the habit data was recorded before the latest rules update — the verified record itself is always current.

A “game” is counted from this team’s side of a battle. “Picked” means chosen among the four Pokémon actually brought to a battle — teams register six, only four play.

Fine print — what these numbers can and can’t say

  • Knockout shares, damage shares, opening moves, and the sim matchup hypotheses come from the fast practice simulator. The slot-weight table uses verified Showdown games when available. The two data sets are labelled with their own game counts because they measure different things — their numbers will not match.
  • Matchup playbooks describe what the team repeatedly chose against each opponent in practice-sim scouting. They do not claim the most-used bring or lead causally outperforms the alternatives.
  • Picked-versus-benched win rates are observational: a Pokémon saved for the hardest matchups can look harmful when it is actually doing the hardest work. A negative swing is a question to investigate, not a verdict.

How to read this report

Two kinds of evidence appear here, and they are not equal.

Verified numbers come from real Pokémon Showdown battles played under the current ruleset — the engine the game is actually played on. These are the numbers that count.

Practice sim numbers come from a fast approximate simulator the lab uses to scout habits: which four get picked, who leads, what moves open the game. Good for reading tendencies, but hypotheses only — a practice-sim number is never proof and is always labelled.

Confidence chips grade the verified sample: Strong evidence means 500+ verified games against 8+ different opponents; Established 200+ against 6+; Still developing 60+ against 3+; Early anything less. “Scouting probe out of date” means the habit data was recorded before the latest rules update — the verified record itself is always current.

A “game” is counted from this team’s side of a battle. “Picked” means chosen among the four Pokémon actually brought to a battle — teams register six, only four play.

Fine print — what these numbers can and can’t say

  • 41,714 Showdown games played under older rules or an older lab setup are kept as historical context only; they do not count toward the verified record or the confidence grade.
  • Knockout shares, damage shares, opening moves, and the sim matchup hypotheses come from the fast practice simulator. The slot-weight table uses verified Showdown games when available. The two data sets are labelled with their own game counts because they measure different things — their numbers will not match.
  • Matchup playbooks describe what the team repeatedly chose against each opponent in practice-sim scouting. They do not claim the most-used bring or lead causally outperforms the alternatives.
  • Picked-versus-benched win rates are observational: a Pokémon saved for the hardest matchups can look harmful when it is actually doing the hardest work. A negative swing is a question to investigate, not a verdict.
  • Older-rules context: 41,714 earlier games at 63.7% won; excluded from the headline record and the confidence grade.

How to read this report

Two kinds of evidence appear here, and they are not equal.

Verified numbers come from real Pokémon Showdown battles played under the current ruleset — the engine the game is actually played on. These are the numbers that count.

Practice sim numbers come from a fast approximate simulator the lab uses to scout habits: which four get picked, who leads, what moves open the game. Good for reading tendencies, but hypotheses only — a practice-sim number is never proof and is always labelled.

Confidence chips grade the verified sample: Strong evidence means 500+ verified games against 8+ different opponents; Established 200+ against 6+; Still developing 60+ against 3+; Early anything less. “Scouting probe out of date” means the habit data was recorded before the latest rules update — the verified record itself is always current.

A “game” is counted from this team’s side of a battle. “Picked” means chosen among the four Pokémon actually brought to a battle — teams register six, only four play.

Fine print — what these numbers can and can’t say

  • 144 Showdown games played under older rules or an older lab setup are kept as historical context only; they do not count toward the verified record or the confidence grade.
  • Knockout shares, damage shares, opening moves, and the sim matchup hypotheses come from the fast practice simulator. The slot-weight table uses verified Showdown games when available. The two data sets are labelled with their own game counts because they measure different things — their numbers will not match.
  • Matchup playbooks describe what the team repeatedly chose against each opponent in practice-sim scouting. They do not claim the most-used bring or lead causally outperforms the alternatives.
  • Picked-versus-benched win rates are observational: a Pokémon saved for the hardest matchups can look harmful when it is actually doing the hardest work. A negative swing is a question to investigate, not a verdict.
  • Older-rules context: 144 earlier games at 68.1% won; excluded from the headline record and the confidence grade.

How to read this report

Two kinds of evidence appear here, and they are not equal.

Verified numbers come from real Pokémon Showdown battles played under the current ruleset — the engine the game is actually played on. These are the numbers that count.

Practice sim numbers come from a fast approximate simulator the lab uses to scout habits: which four get picked, who leads, what moves open the game. Good for reading tendencies, but hypotheses only — a practice-sim number is never proof and is always labelled.

Confidence chips grade the verified sample: Strong evidence means 500+ verified games against 8+ different opponents; Established 200+ against 6+; Still developing 60+ against 3+; Early anything less. “Scouting probe out of date” means the habit data was recorded before the latest rules update — the verified record itself is always current.

A “game” is counted from this team’s side of a battle. “Picked” means chosen among the four Pokémon actually brought to a battle — teams register six, only four play.

Fine print — what these numbers can and can’t say

  • 13,594 Showdown games played under older rules or an older lab setup are kept as historical context only; they do not count toward the verified record or the confidence grade.
  • Knockout shares, damage shares, opening moves, and the sim matchup hypotheses come from the fast practice simulator. The slot-weight table uses verified Showdown games when available. The two data sets are labelled with their own game counts because they measure different things — their numbers will not match.
  • Matchup playbooks describe what the team repeatedly chose against each opponent in practice-sim scouting. They do not claim the most-used bring or lead causally outperforms the alternatives.
  • Picked-versus-benched win rates are observational: a Pokémon saved for the hardest matchups can look harmful when it is actually doing the hardest work. A negative swing is a question to investigate, not a verdict.
  • Older-rules context: 13,594 earlier games at 63.0% won; excluded from the headline record and the confidence grade.
